subject: ENGRD
course_description: Introduction to rhetoric and rhetorical analysis. While learning rhetorical tactics of Ancient Greece and Rome, students will apply that learning to their academic and vocational goals. Practice in writing and speaking, grounded in ethics, are central to the course.
course_notes: Close Listening: How do (or don't) we talk to each other? How can we effectively express our ideas to one another? What moments make it seem as though language "fails" us, and how do we navigate that tension? This class takes up those queries through locating the primacy of sound in how we present ourselves and our arguments to specific audiences. Instead of overemphasizing what we say, this class will investigate creative, sonic-based ways to communicate, taking Black and queer rhetoricians as our core interlocutors to think through not only how we use language but how language uses us. A variation on a theme of the "close reading" methodology customary to English departments, close listening will be our primary operative to equip us to rigorously analyze texts, form arguments about them, and, fundamentally, create space to hear what they really have to say. Pairing written work with visual and aural storytelling, we will think alongside artists including but not limited to James Baldwin, Toni Morrison, Percival Everett, Audre Lorde, Natasha Trethewey, Ryan Coogler, Ralph Ellison, Gayl Jones, Jordan Peele, and Janelle Monae. In class viewings of films/tv episodes and hands-on writing activities are likely. Students will leave the course knowing not only how to build arguments and express themselves more effectively but also, fundamentally, how to listen.
